result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_corona()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Extract the k-corona subgraph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28332-L28410){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_corona(k) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-corona](/assets/graphs/k-corona.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the eight-node graph with a dense cluster A to D, a ring E, F, G and a pendant H. Right: the 2-corona keeps the 2-core nodes with exactly two neighbors in the 2-core, F and G with their edge in the accent color. E is in the 2-core too but has three such neighbors, so it is dashed along with the rest." width="100%"} The k-corona is the subgraph induced by nodes that are in the k-core and have exactly `k` neighbors in the k-core. These are the "boundary" nodes of the k-core that would be removed first when computing the `(k+1)`-core. The k-corona helps identify nodes at the periphery of dense substructures, which is useful for understanding hierarchical organization and vulnerability analysis. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The core number. Nodes in the k-corona have coreness >= `k` and exactly `k` neighbors within the k-core. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-corona nodes and their connecting edges. May be empty if no nodes satisfy the k-corona criteria. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The $k$-corona sits inside the $k$-shell (nodes with coreness exactly $k$) and picks out just those members that are *marginally* attached: they participate in the $k$-core but have precisely $k$ neighbors there, so losing any one of those neighbors would drop them out. Because that fragility is what defines the peeling order in $k$-core decomposition, the $k$-corona corresponds exactly to the batch of nodes stripped away in the very next round when computing the $(k + 1)$-core. It can be empty even when the $k$-shell is non-empty, and it is the natural set to inspect for structurally vulnerable positions inside dense subgraphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Find the 2-corona in a simple graph: ::: {#6550d36b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create a graph with a dense core and peripheral nodes g = ec.Graph() # Dense core: nodes 1, 2, 3 form a triangle g.add_nodes(["1", "2", "3"]) g.add_edges([("1", "2"), ("2", "3"), ("3", "1")]) # Add peripheral nodes g.add_nodes(["4", "5"]) g.add_edges([("1", "4"), ("2", "5")]) # The 2-corona contains nodes in the 2-core with exactly 2 neighbors in 2-core corona_2 = g.k_corona(2) # Returns the number of nodes in the 2-corona corona_2.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Analyze hierarchical structure: ::: {#58d57b10 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Build a graph and examine different corona levels g = ec.Graph() g.add_full_graph(5) # K5 complete graph # In K5, all nodes have degree 4, so they're in the 4-core # Each node has exactly 4 neighbors in the 4-core corona_4 = g.k_corona(4) # Returns 5 (all 5 nodes are in the 4-corona) corona_4.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 5 ``` ::: :::
